full_judgment:
3. The defendants contested the suit by filling a joint written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit was bad for defect of parties; that the answering defendants have no concern with the overdraft granted to the late Halima Khatoon; that the answering defendants have not furnished any security or guarantee against the alleged loan of Halima Khatoon; that the plaintiff-Bank granted overdraft to the extent of Tk. 70,000.00 on 12.12.70 on receipt of NIT certificates worth Tk. 84,330.00 and the said loan was repayable by 31.12.71 and, as such the suit was barred by limitation; that the said Halima Khatoon died on 8.3.72 leaving bahind her husband, defendant No. 1, 4 sons including defendant No. 2 and 3 and daughters, but the plaintiff did not make all her heirs parties to the suit. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the suit was maintainable in its present form; that the suit was not barred by limitation; that the NIT certificates were not en cashable by the plaintiff-Bank and that the defendants were liable for the money claimed. Upon these findings the learned subordinate Judge decreed the suit against the defendant- appellants for an amount of Tk. 1,07,099.00 with interest at the rate of 20% from the date of institution of the suit. Hence this appeal by the defendants. 

 6. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellants, has contended that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in not holding that the suit was barred by limitation and, as such, the decree was liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate has also submitted that the borrower having died the suit should have been filed against all her legal heirs to the extent of the property they inherited from her but the plaintiff-Bank instituted the suit against her husband and only one son and as such the suit was not maintainable. 

 7. Since the main question in this appeal centred round the question of limitation and since the trial Court did not consider the question of defect of parties we like to confine ourselves to the question of limitation in disposing of the appeal. 

 8. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the appellants submitted that the suit was governed by article 57 of the Limitation Act inasmuch as the suit was for recovery of money secured by pledge and he had relied upon the case of Percy F. Fisher Vs. Ardeshir Hormasji Gazdar and another reported in AIR 1935 (Bom) 213 and the case of Babu Monmohan Das Vs. Baldeo Narain Tendon and others reported in AIR 1938 (Privy Council) 66 in support of his contention. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent Bank, on the other hand, has contended that the suit was governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act and relied upon the case of Mahalinga Nadar Vs. Vanapathi Subbien reported in ILR 27 (Mad) 528 (Full Bench). 

 10. Article 57 of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act provides that limitation for a suit for money payable for money lent is 3 years from the date when the loan is made. According to Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the appellants, the present suit is governed by this article 57 of the Limitation Act. and as the loan was advanced in 1971 and the suit was filed in 1981, the suit is barred by limitation. According to the learned Advocate, even if the balance as on 31.12.76 is taken as the date for the money lent still the suit is barred having been filed beyond 3 years from that date. The case referred to by the learned Advocate reported in AIR 1935 (Bom) 213 is a suit filed in the original side of the High Court to recover a sum of money with interest for money lent and advanced to the defendants at different times in 1920 and for an order for sale of certain shares alleged to have been pledged with the plaintiff in January, 1922 as security for repayment of the loan advanced to him. It was held therein by a learned Single Judge that the period of limitation for a suit to recover money lent and advanced is 3 years under article 57 of the Limitation Act. The second case referred to by Mr. Hossain is the case reported in AIR 1938 (Privy Council) 66 wherein it was held that the article 57 of the Limitation Act was applicable to a suit for recovery of money payable for the money lent. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent-Bank, on the other hand, has referred to the case reported in ILR 27 (Mad.) 528 (Full Bench). In that case the plaintiff lent money on the pledged Jewels and filed the suit more than 3 years and less than 6 years from the date of the pledge to recover the amount lent, by sale of the jewels and it was held therein that the claim is governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act, wherein the limitation is 6 years to proceed against the property pledged. But the instant suit before us is not to proceed against the pledged property. It may be mentioned that in the case reported in AIR 1935 (Bom) 213 it has also been held that under a pledge, right to sue on the security in default of payment is governed by article 120. In this case before us the NIT Certificates were pledged with the Bank in 1971, beyond a period of 6 years from the date of institution of the suit. 

 11. In our view neither article 57 nor article 12 is applicable to the instant case. But it is article 85 of the Limitation Act which applies to the present case, inasmuch as the suit to which article 85 applies is a suit "for the balance due on a mutual open and current account where there have been reciprocal demands between the parties" and the limitation is 3 years from "the close of the year, in which the last item admitted or proved is entered in the-account". In our view, the present suit is one for balance due on mutual, open and current account and the limitation is 3 years from the close of the year in which the last transaction was made. Reference may be made to the case of the Reliance Bank Limited Vs. Profullah Kumar Banerjee reported in 5 DLR 69 PLD 1953 (Dacca) 220, PLR 1952 (Dhaka) 342 wherein a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court held, relying on the case of the Tea Financing Syndicate Ltd. Vs. Chandra Kamal Bez Barua reported in AIR 1931 (Calcutta) 359-34 CWN 1175-52 CLJ 314, the case of Kars o n d a s Dhunjibhoy Vs. Surajbhun Ramrijpal and others reported in AIR 1933 (Bom) 450, ILR 58 (Born) 200 and the case of RN Kapur, partner of Messrs Wright and Co. Vs. Tranvancore National and Quilon Bank Ltd. reported in AIR 1945 (Mad) 467, that when a person opens a current account with a bank and pays money into it, the bank is a debtor to the customer; if the bank allows the customer to overdraw the account and he does so, he becomes debtor to the bank and each party could say that he had a separate account against the other one being in respect of the current account and the other being in respect of the overdraft account; that there was independent obligation of each party arising from each account and that on the basis of the balance of each account the balance of the other could be set off; and a case of this nature is governed by article 85 of the Limitation Act. 

 12. In the case reported in 5 DLR 69 the plaintiff-Bank instituted the suit for recovery of a certain amount alleged to have been due under open and mutual account together with the facilities for overdraft opened at the instance of the defendant. In that case the defendant who was carrying on rice business opened a current account with the plaintiff-bank on 5.9.37 and for facilities of his rice business obtained overdraft facilities by executing a promissory note for Tk. 8000.00 in favour of the bank and by way of additional security hypothecated stock of rice lying in his godown. The defendant denied that the current account was a mutual one and pleaded that the suit was barred by limitation. It was noticed by their Lordships that the last transaction was made on 21.10.1941 and held that the suit was not barred by limitation as the same was instituted in 1944. In that case it was held that article 83 is applicable in case of mutual open current account in banking transaction and their Lordships quoted the following passage from AIR 1945 (Mad) 467: 

 13. In the instant case before us late Halima Khatoon had an account with the bank and she asked for overdraft facilities and there were number of transactions by withdrawal of amounts or deposit of amounts which continued till 10.12.71 which is the last item of the transaction between the parties. As such we hold that article 85 of the Limitation Act will govern the present suit and period of limitation is 3 years from the close of the year in which the last item of transaction was made. As has been mentioned the last item of the transaction between the parties was on 10.12.71 and, as such, the period of limitation is 3 years from 31.12.71; but the suit was filed beyond 3 years from that date on 28.5.81. The exclusion of the period from 1st of March, 1971 to 1st of March, 1972 under President's Order 12 of 1972 is of no consequence in the present case. 

 14. Similar view was taken by a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court in the case of Nabadwip Chandra Podder and another Vs. SD Ahmed reported in 21 DLR 755. In that case the Liquidator of the Das Bank Limited instituted suit for recovery of certain amount on the allegation that the defendants used to carry on jute business at Bhairab Bazer and for the purpose of obtaining facilities from the Bank, the defendants opened an overdraft account in their names in the Bhairab Bazar branch of the Bank in 1941. According to the Bank's ledger the last transaction between the parties was on 22.7.47 and upon an application for winding up of the Bank the Dhaka High Court made an order on 26.5.50 winding up the Bank; and it was held therein that at the date of institution of the suit on 31.12.56 the disputed account was no longer a mutual, open and current account, the same having been closed long ago. It was further held therein that in order to attract the application of article 85 of the Limitation Act it is necessary that the account must be subsisting at the date of the suit. 

 15. Thus, considering the facts and circumstances of the present case, we hold that the suit is governed by article 85 of the Limitation Act and we further hold that the suit is barred by limitation.
